name: Ashwagandha

identity.whatItIs: An evergreen shrub from parts of India, Africa and the Middle East, sold as root and leaf supplements.

oneLineAnswer: An Ayurvedic shrub root sold as a stress and sleep supplement; trials are small but some show real effects.
whatItDoes: Ashwagandha is an evergreen shrub from India, Africa and the Middle East, sold as root or leaf supplements.
Those plant parts contain withanolides, a compound group studied for anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activity.
US federal reviewers at NCCIH report that some ashwagandha preparations may help with insomnia and stress.
The same review calls the evidence on anxiety unclear, and says most other uses remain unproven.
It also reports limited evidence that two to four months of use may raise testosterone and sperm quality.
whatWeDoNotKnow: No one knows what ashwagandha does to the body over the long term.
NCCIH says there is not enough information to judge safety beyond about three months.
Results for one product may not carry over to another.
Trials have used different root, leaf and extract preparations, often in small groups of people.
The sources do not give a liver-injury rate for ashwagandha users, so the risk size is unknown.
It is still unproven for asthma, athletic performance, thinking and memory, diabetes, menopause and female infertility.
Claims that it treats COVID-19 are not supported by high-quality evidence.
Registered trials cover stress, sleep, stress-hormone activity, weight and sexual health.
No posted results were read for those trials, so no effect sizes are reported here.

safetyNotes.text: NCCIH states short-term use, up to about three months, may be safe, but long-term safety is not established.
Reported effects in some people include drowsiness, stomach upset, diarrhea and vomiting.
NCCIH notes that rare case reports have linked liver injury to ashwagandha supplements.
NCCIH says ashwagandha should be avoided during pregnancy and while breastfeeding.
NCCIH does not recommend it before surgery, or for people with autoimmune or thyroid disorders.
NCCIH lists possible interactions with diabetes and blood pressure medicines, immunosuppressants, sedatives, anti-seizure medicines and thyroid hormones.
NCCIH says people with hormone-sensitive prostate cancer should avoid it, because it may raise testosterone.
A prescription label warns that ashwagandha may increase the effects of sedatives and several other medicines. It names blood pressure, diabetes, thyroid and immunosuppressive medicines.
Some over-the-counter products carrying ashwagandha are homeopathic combination liquids. Their labels say the claims rest on traditional homeopathic practice, not accepted medical evidence.

confidenceRationale: Two independent fetched sources (NCCIH and ClinicalTrials.gov) support the descriptive and research-activity claims, and a third (openFDA labels) independently supports the medicine-interaction caution. Confidence is not set to high because the efficacy direction for stress and sleep rests on the single NCCIH review, no trial result data was read, and no second narrative review was available inside the permitted source list.
gaps: ClinicalTrials.gov registrations show trials exist, but posted results were not fetched, so no effect sizes, p-values or between-group differences are reported here.
The NCCIH summary is the only narrative review available in the permitted source list. Its page carries a March 2023 last-updated date.

MedlinePlus has no ashwagandha health topic page; https://medlineplus.gov/ashwagandha.html returned HTTP 404, and https://medlineplus.gov/herbalmedicine.html does not mention ashwagandha. MedlinePlus therefore grounded nothing. No MedlinePlus drug monograph URLs were fetched.
PubChem has no ashwagandha monograph page. The withanolide chemistry claim is grounded through the Withaferin A compound record instead.

openFDA returned only multi-ingredient labels containing ashwagandha (homeopathic combination liquids and one prescription multivitamin), not an ashwagandha drug monograph, so label-based claims are product-specific.
The openFDA query for brand_name "Ashwagandha" returned no results.
No incidence rate, dose-response or product-comparison data for the reported liver injury signal was available in the sources checked.
No general dosing content is included. The sources checked give only manufacturer-specific product directions, which is not a basis for advice.
Whether ashwagandha helps with asthma, athletic performance, cognition, diabetes, menopause, female infertility or obesity remains ungrounded beyond statements that evidence is insufficient.
Verbatim quotes were trimmed only where a source sentence exceeded 25 words; one clinical trial JSON quote preserves raw API punctuation.
editorialPolicy: Original prose written by rnawiki from facts observed in public-domain and CC0 sources. No source sentence was reproduced as page text; every factual claim carries a bounded verbatim quote for verification. No individualised dosing, diagnosis or treatment advice is included. Copyrighted sources (MedlinePlus drug monographs, Examine.com, Labdoor, MSKCC About Herbs, ConsumerLab, WebMD, Healthline, Drugs.com, RxList) were neither fetched nor used.
